questions.question: Study the memory layout shown. A class Resource has int* data. Without a custom copy constructor, what happens during MyFunc(Resource r)?
options: A deep copy is made — r.data points to its own heap memory
A shallow copy is made — r.data points to the same heap memory as the original; if r's destructor frees data, the original object's pointer becomes dangling
No copy is made — the function receives a reference automatically
The compiler refuses to compile without an explicit copy constructor
questions.answer: A shallow copy is made — r.data points to the same heap memory as the original; if r's destructor frees data, the original object's pointer becomes dangling

diagramData.representation: Original obj: data ptr=0x400 (heap). Pass-by-value creates copy r: r.data=0x400 (same heap). MyFunc returns: ~r() called, frees 0x400. Original obj.data now dangling at freed 0x400.

values.consequence: original.data now dangling — UB on access

Members are always initialized in the order they are declared in the class body, regardless of initializer list order — relying on list order is a common bug
Members are initialized in reverse declaration order
The order depends on whether members are public or private
questions.answer: Members are always initialized in the order they are declared in the class body, regardless of initializer list order — relying on list order is a common bug

diagramData.representation: class T { int a; int b; T():b(10),a(b+1){} }. Declaration order: a first, then b. Init: a initialized first (b not yet set -> UB/garbage), then b=10. Initializer list order b,a is misleading.

values.rule: init order follows DECLARATION order, not list order

Move and copy constructors are always called together

questions.question: Observe the pointer layout. When should you use weak_ptr instead of shared_ptr?
options: weak_ptr should be used when you need to guarantee the object stays alive

weak_ptr breaks circular reference cycles — it holds a non-owning reference that does not increment the reference count; use it when an object needs to observe a shared resource without preventing its deletion
weak_ptr automatically converts to a raw pointer when the object is deleted
weak_ptr is only used with unique_ptr, not shared_ptr
questions.answer: weak_ptr breaks circular reference cycles — it holds a non-owning reference that does not increment the reference count; use it when an object needs to observe a shared resource without preventing its deletion

diagramData.representation: Circular: shared_ptr<A> a owns B; shared_ptr<B> b owns A -> ref counts never reach 0 -> memory leak. Fix: one direction uses weak_ptr<A> -> does not increment A's ref count -> when external shared_ptrs release, ref count reaches 0 and both are freed.

values.result: A freed when external shared_ptr<A> gone; B freed after

questions.question: What is the difference between early binding and late binding in C++?
options: They are synonyms for the same mechanism

Early binding (static dispatch) resolves function calls at compile time for non-virtual, static, and overloaded functions; late binding (dynamic dispatch) resolves virtual function calls at runtime via vtable, enabling polymorphism
Late binding is always faster than early binding
Early binding only applies to constructor calls
questions.answer: Early binding (static dispatch) resolves function calls at compile time for non-virtual, static, and overloaded functions; late binding (dynamic dispatch) resolves virtual function calls at runtime via vtable, enabling polymorphism

questions.question: What is object slicing in C++ and when does it occur?
options: Object slicing is a memory optimization that removes unused base members

Object slicing occurs when a derived class object is assigned or copied to a base class object by value — the derived-class-specific members are 'sliced off', leaving only the base portion; polymorphism is lost
Object slicing only affects static data members
Object slicing is prevented automatically by using virtual functions
questions.answer: Object slicing occurs when a derived class object is assigned or copied to a base class object by value — the derived-class-specific members are 'sliced off', leaving only the base portion; polymorphism is lost

questions.question: What is the difference between a class's interface and its implementation in OOP?
options: Interface and implementation are the same in C++ — there is no separation

The interface is the public contract (member function declarations, access specifiers) that clients depend on; the implementation is the private internal logic — separating them allows changing internals without breaking client code (encapsulation)
Interface in C++ can only be defined using pure virtual functions
Implementation refers only to the constructor body
questions.answer: The interface is the public contract (member function declarations, access specifiers) that clients depend on; the implementation is the private internal logic — separating them allows changing internals without breaking client code (encapsulation)

questions.question: What is the significance of the 'mutable' keyword in C++?
options: mutable makes a variable a compile-time constant

mutable allows a specific data member to be modified even inside a const member function — useful for caching or lazy evaluation where internal state changes do not logically affect the observable state
mutable is equivalent to volatile and forces memory reads from hardware
mutable prevents a member from being copied during object assignment
questions.answer: mutable allows a specific data member to be modified even inside a const member function — useful for caching or lazy evaluation where internal state changes do not logically affect the observable state

questions.question: What is encapsulation in C++ and how is it achieved?
options: Encapsulation means all class members must be public

Encapsulation is the bundling of data and the functions that operate on it into a single unit (class), and restricting direct access to internal state using private/protected access specifiers — exposing only a controlled public interface
Encapsulation means a class can only have one data member
Encapsulation is only achieved through inheritance
questions.answer: Encapsulation is the bundling of data and the functions that operate on it into a single unit (class), and restricting direct access to internal state using private/protected access specifiers — exposing only a controlled public interface

questions.question: What is abstraction in C++ and how does it differ from encapsulation?
options: Abstraction and encapsulation are identical concepts

Abstraction hides complexity by exposing only relevant features to the user (what an object does); encapsulation hides the internal implementation details (how it does it) — abstraction is achieved via abstract classes and interfaces
Abstraction only applies to template classes
Encapsulation is a superset of abstraction with no practical difference
questions.answer: Abstraction hides complexity by exposing only relevant features to the user (what an object does); encapsulation hides the internal implementation details (how it does it) — abstraction is achieved via abstract classes and interfaces

questions.question: What is a parameterized constructor in C++ and why is it used?
options: A constructor that takes no parameters and initializes all members to zero
A constructor that accepts arguments to initialize object members with specific values at creation time — allows different objects of the same class to be initialized with different data
A constructor that can only be called with a single integer argument
A constructor automatically generated by the compiler for every class
questions.answer: A constructor that accepts arguments to initialize object members with specific values at creation time — allows different objects of the same class to be initialized with different data

questions.question: What is a constructor initializer list and why is it preferred over assignment inside the constructor body?
options: Initializer lists are only required for static members

An initializer list initializes members directly before the constructor body executes — required for const members, reference members, and base classes; also more efficient since it avoids default-construction followed by assignment
Initializer lists execute after the constructor body
Initializer lists can only be used with primitive data types
questions.answer: An initializer list initializes members directly before the constructor body executes — required for const members, reference members, and base classes; also more efficient since it avoids default-construction followed by assignment

questions.question: What is the difference between break and continue statements in loops?
options: break and continue both terminate the loop immediately
break exits the loop entirely; continue skips the rest of the current iteration and jumps to the next iteration's condition check
continue exits the loop; break skips only the current iteration
break is only valid in switch; continue is only valid in for loops
questions.answer: break exits the loop entirely; continue skips the rest of the current iteration and jumps to the next iteration's condition check

questions.question: What is a 1D array and how is it stored in memory in C++?
options: A 1D array stores elements at random memory locations linked by pointers
A 1D array stores elements of the same type in contiguous memory locations — the array name decays to a pointer to the first element; element i is at base_address + i * sizeof(element_type)
A 1D array can store elements of different types
C++ 1D arrays always require dynamic allocation with new[]
questions.answer: A 1D array stores elements of the same type in contiguous memory locations — the array name decays to a pointer to the first element; element i is at base_address + i * sizeof(element_type)

questions.question: What is a 2D array in C++ and how are its elements accessed?
options: A 2D array is a linked list of 1D arrays
A 2D array is a matrix stored in row-major order in contiguous memory — element [i][j] is at base_address + (i * cols + j) * sizeof(type); accessed with double subscript arr[i][j]
A 2D array stores rows in separate heap allocations
2D arrays cannot be passed to functions in C++
questions.answer: A 2D array is a matrix stored in row-major order in contiguous memory — element [i][j] is at base_address + (i * cols + j) * sizeof(type); accessed with double subscript arr[i][j]

questions.question: What are command-line arguments in C++ and how are they accessed in main()?
options: Command-line arguments are environment variables read from the OS registry

Command-line arguments are passed via int argc (argument count including program name) and char* argv[] (array of C-strings) — argv[0] is the program name, argv[1] onward are the user-supplied arguments
argc counts only the user-supplied arguments, excluding the program name
Command-line arguments can only be integers in C++
questions.answer: Command-line arguments are passed via int argc (argument count including program name) and char* argv[] (array of C-strings) — argv[0] is the program name, argv[1] onward are the user-supplied arguments

questions.question: What is a scope resolution operator :: in C++ and what are its uses?
options: :: is only used to access global variables

:: accesses class static members (ClassName::member), defines member functions outside the class (ClassName::func), accesses global scope when shadowed by a local variable (::var), and accesses namespace members (std::cout)
:: is only valid for namespace access
:: can only be used inside class definitions
questions.answer: :: accesses class static members (ClassName::member), defines member functions outside the class (ClassName::func), accesses global scope when shadowed by a local variable (::var), and accesses namespace members (std::cout)

questions.question: What is a constant member function in C++ and what does it guarantee?
options: A const member function can only be called on const objects with no other restriction
A const member function (declared with const after the parameter list) guarantees it will not modify any non-mutable data members of the object — it can be called on both const and non-const objects
A const member function cannot have a return value
A const member function makes all its parameters const automatically
questions.answer: A const member function (declared with const after the parameter list) guarantees it will not modify any non-mutable data members of the object — it can be called on both const and non-const objects

questions.question: What is the difference between the STL stack and queue containers?
options: stack and queue both provide random access to elements
stack is LIFO (Last In First Out) — access via top()/push()/pop(); queue is FIFO (First In First Out) — access via front()/push()/pop(); neither supports random access by index
queue is LIFO; stack is FIFO
Both stack and queue are identical with different names
questions.answer: stack is LIFO (Last In First Out) — access via top()/push()/pop(); queue is FIFO (First In First Out) — access via front()/push()/pop(); neither supports random access by index

questions.question: What is call-by-reference in C++ and what advantage does it have over call-by-value?
options: Call-by-reference passes a copy of the variable to the function

Call-by-reference passes the actual variable's alias — changes inside the function affect the original, and no copy is made, reducing overhead for large objects; useful when the function must modify the caller's variable
Call-by-reference is identical to passing a pointer
Call-by-reference is only valid for primitive types in C++
questions.answer: Call-by-reference passes the actual variable's alias — changes inside the function affect the original, and no copy is made, reducing overhead for large objects; useful when the function must modify the caller's variable

questions.question: What is the purpose of the #include preprocessor directive in C++?
options: #include executes code from another file at runtime

#include instructs the preprocessor to textually insert the contents of the specified header file at that point in the source before compilation — making declarations, class definitions, and function prototypes available
#include links object files during the linking phase
#include is only needed for user-defined header files, not standard library headers
questions.answer: #include instructs the preprocessor to textually insert the contents of the specified header file at that point in the source before compilation — making declarations, class definitions, and function prototypes available

questions.question: What is a friend function in C++ and what is its access privilege?
options: A friend function is a member function that can access private members of other classes

A friend function is a non-member function declared with the friend keyword inside a class — it is granted access to the class's private and protected members, useful for operator overloading and tightly coupled utility functions
A friend function is always a static member of the class
A friend function can only access public members of the class
questions.answer: A friend function is a non-member function declared with the friend keyword inside a class — it is granted access to the class's private and protected members, useful for operator overloading and tightly coupled utility functions

questions.question: What is the difference between prefix and postfix increment operators in C++?
options: Both prefix and postfix return the incremented value
Prefix ++x increments x and returns the new (incremented) value; postfix x++ saves the original value, increments x, then returns the original value — postfix creates a temporary copy
Postfix ++x increments x and returns new value; prefix x++ returns old value
They are identical and produce the same result in all contexts
questions.answer: Prefix ++x increments x and returns the new (incremented) value; postfix x++ saves the original value, increments x, then returns the original value — postfix creates a temporary copy

questions.question: What is the C++ Standard Library and what are its main categories?
options: The Standard Library is an optional add-on that must be downloaded separately

The C++ Standard Library is a collection of classes and functions specified by the ISO C++ standard — main categories include the STL (containers, algorithms, iterators), I/O streams, strings, numerics, threading utilities, and smart pointers
The Standard Library only provides input/output stream classes
The Standard Library is identical to the C Standard Library with no additions
questions.answer: The C++ Standard Library is a collection of classes and functions specified by the ISO C++ standard — main categories include the STL (containers, algorithms, iterators), I/O streams, strings, numerics, threading utilities, and smart pointers
